652.title: Where death is, I am not
652.hook: Epicurus: death is nothing to us, for when we are, death is not (Letter to Menoeceus)
652.howItsDone: Epicureans have long repeated the teaching that death is nothing to us as a remedy for the fear of being dead, and the Latin epitaph 'I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care' appears on many Roman tombs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bread and water, the plain meal that tastes best when you're hungry. Your line was bread and water. What did your plain meal taste like? Day six hundred fifty-two.

On some old Roman gravestones, archaeologists keep finding the same short line, sometimes just as initials. In Latin it runs: I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care. It sounds bleak at first. Then strangely calm. Whoever carved it was likely echoing a teaching from the Garden, an argument Epicurus made to his friend Menoeceus about the thing people fear most. The argument fits in a single sentence, and people are still arguing with it. Today: where death is, I am not.
screen: `I WAS NOT, I WAS, I AM NOT.` → `I DON'T CARE.` → `THE ARGUMENT FROM THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says: get used to thinking that death is nothing to us. Why? Because everything good and bad is a matter of feeling, and death is the end of feeling. So while we are, death is not here; and when death is here, we are not. It never meets us. Second, the fear it's aimed at. Epicurus wasn't trying to make dying painless, or losing someone easy. He was aiming at a specific dread: the fear of being dead, of some terrible state afterward. If there's no one there to suffer it, he says, there's nothing to fear in it. Third, a later echo. The Roman poet Lucretius, an Epicurean, added a second picture: think of all the time before you were born. It didn't trouble you. The time after you die, he said, is a mirror of it. Fourth, honesty about where people stand. Epicurus's argument depends on his belief that the soul is made of atoms and scatters at death. Many people, in many traditions, believe something continues after death, and find comfort there instead. Others, especially in the Garden's tradition, find comfort exactly here, in nothing to fear. The path doesn't settle that. It notices that thoughtful people for two thousand years have found this one sentence steadying, or troubling, or both. Either way, it asks something useful: is it death you fear, or something about living, like unfinished things, or leaving people behind? Those, at least, can be worked on today.

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe gently. If this topic is heavy for you today, you can simply follow the breath instead. If you're willing, hold Epicurus's sentence lightly: while I am, death is not; when death is, I am not. Don't decide whether you agree. Just notice what it stirs. Calm? Resistance? Something else? Then ask, quietly: underneath, what am I actually afraid of? Let the answer come in its own words, and notice whether it's something you can tend to while you're here. The bell holds the time.

Your line: where death is, I'm not. Today, do one thing on the unfinished list you'd be sorry to leave undone. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: Friends above all
653.hook: Epicurus: of all wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest is friendship (Principal Doctrines 27)
653.howItsDone: Epicureans, ancient and modern, place friendship at the center of a good life, sharing meals, keeping in touch and caring for one another's families.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where death is, I am not, Epicurus's one-sentence argument. Your line was where death is, I'm not. What did you finish from the unfinished list? Day six hundred fifty-three.

Before you choose a restaurant, do you think about the food, or about who's coming? Epicurus had a firm answer. Seneca, a Stoic who loved to quote him, passes it on in one of his letters: look first for whom you'll eat and drink with, before you look at what you'll eat and drink. Eating alone, without a friend, he says, is the life of a lion or a wolf. Strong words from a man known for simple food. Today, the Garden's center. Friends above all.
screen: `THE FOOD, OR WHO'S COMING?` → `FIRST: WHOM YOU'LL EAT WITH.` → `FRIENDS ABOVE ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the doctrine. Epicurus left forty short sayings, the Principal Doctrines, meant to be memorized. Number twenty-seven says, in plain words: of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. Not knowledge. Not money. Not even calm on its own. Friends. Second, why a philosopher of pleasure ranks it first. Epicurus said a friendship may begin from need: someone helps you, you help them. But it becomes worth having for its own sake. And it carries something else: confidence. Another saying of his puts it this way: it isn't so much our friends' help that helps us, as our trust that they'd help if we needed it. That trust takes a great deal of fear out of life. Third, how the Garden lived it. Diogenes Laërtius says Epicurus had so many friends that whole cities couldn't count them. His school ate together, kept birthdays together, and wrote letters across the Greek world. In his will, Epicurus provided for a yearly gathering of friends, and for the children of a friend who had died. Fourth, the neighbor's answer. The Stoics also prized friendship, but they called it a good only between people of virtue, and wanted the wise person to be able to stand alone if friends were lost. Epicurus wanted friendship close to the center of the good life. Two schools, both serious about friends, weighting them differently. And either way, a good meal with no one across the table was, to Epicurus, hardly a meal at all.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the faces of your friends come to mind, one at a time, no ranking. The one who always answers. The one you laugh with. The one who's drifted. Notice which face makes you feel safe, which makes you smile, which makes you miss something. Now settle on the drifted one, or the one you've been too busy for. Imagine sending them a message. What would it say? Keep it simple. Let the warmth of that friendship sit in your chest. The bell holds the time.
Friends above all. Epicurus taught that of everything wisdom gives for a happy life, friendship is by far the greatest. Today's word.

654.title: Borrowing from rivals
654.hook: Seneca quotes Epicurus often, taking good ideas from a rival school (Letters 2–29)
654.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's letters notice how often he closes with a saying from Epicurus, and many take it as a model for learning from rival views while keeping one's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: friends above all, Epicurus's greatest gift of wisdom, passed on by Seneca. Your line was friendship first. Did the drifted friend write back? Day six hundred fifty-four.

Picture a fan of one team quietly studying the other team's playbook, admiring it, and taking notes. Or someone deep in one political camp who reads the other side's best writer every week. Most of us don't do that. It feels like betrayal. We read people who already agree with us, and we read the other side mostly to find what's wrong. Seneca, a committed Stoic, did something different, over and over, in letters we've been reading all year. He kept quoting the founder of the rival school. Today: borrowing from rivals.
screen: `STUDYING THE OTHER TEAM'S PLAYBOOK.` → `IT FEELS LIKE BETRAYAL.` → `SENECA QUOTES THE RIVAL.`

segments.voice: First, the habit. In his early letters to his friend Lucilius, Seneca ends almost every one with a small gift: a saying to take away. And again and again, the saying comes from Epicurus, head of the Garden, the school Stoics argued against on gods, nature, pleasure and death. Second, how he explains it. In Letter 2, Seneca says he likes to cross into the enemy's camp, in Richard Gummere's translation, "not as a deserter, but as a scout." He isn't switching sides. He's going over to bring back what's useful. Then the gift from Epicurus that day: that contented poverty is an honorable state. Third, his principle. Lucilius seems to have teased him about it. Seneca answers, across several letters, that a true and well-said thing belongs to everyone; the best ideas are public property, whoever said them first. He'll take a good line from anyone. Fourth, what he doesn't do. He doesn't pretend the schools agree. He keeps his own Stoic views, and later in the letters he argues hard against Epicurean ideas. Borrowing a good thing isn't the same as giving up your own ground. And respecting a rival's insight isn't the same as pretending your differences don't matter. That's harder than either cheering your side or abandoning it. It means holding your convictions and keeping your ears open, at the same time.
screen: `A GIFT AT THE END OF EACH LETTER.` · `NOT A DESERTER, BUT A SCOUT.` · `A TRUE THING BELONGS TO EVERYONE.` · `BORROW WITHOUT GIVING UP GROUND.` · then, large: `BORROW THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you disagree with, a relative, a writer, a coworker, someone from the other side of something. Let the disagreement be there; you don't have to resolve it. Now, like a scout, look for one thing they get right. One value, one insight, one fair point. It may take a moment. Stay curious. When you find it, hold it up and look at it, without giving up anything of your own. The bell holds the time.
Borrowing from rivals. Seneca, a Stoic, kept quoting Epicurus, crossing into the rival camp as a scout, not a deserter. Today's word.
Your line: borrow the good. Today, read or listen to one thing from someone you usually disagree with, and keep one good line from it. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: The skeptics
655.hook: Pyrrho's followers suspended judgment and found calm in not deciding
655.howItsDone: Pyrrhonian skeptics practiced suspending judgment, weighing opposing arguments until they balanced, and living by appearances and custom without claiming final truth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: borrowing from rivals, Seneca crossing into Epicurus's camp as a scout. Your line was borrow the good. What good line did you keep? Day six hundred fifty-five.

A painter is trying to paint a horse, and he can't get the foam at its mouth right. He tries and tries. Finally, furious, he throws his sponge at the canvas. Where it hits, it leaves a mark, and the mark looks exactly like foam. The story was told by an ancient doctor and philosopher named Sextus Empiricus, and he told it to explain something odd: how peace of mind arrived for his school the moment they stopped trying to grab it. Today: the skeptics.
screen: `A PAINTER, A HORSE, THE FOAM.` → `HE THROWS THE SPONGE.` → `PEACE ARRIVES WHEN YOU STOP GRABBING.`

segments.voice: First, the founder. Pyrrho of Elis lived around the time of Alexander the Great and, according to Diogenes Laërtius, traveled with Alexander's army as far as India, where he met local sages. He wrote nothing. Later followers took his name: Pyrrhonists. Wild stories were told about him, that friends had to pull him out of the way of carts because he wouldn't trust his senses. Even some ancient writers doubted those. Second, the method. The skeptics noticed that for almost any claim, you can find an argument against it that seems just as strong. Is honey sweet? To you, yes; to someone sick, bitter. So they practiced epochē: suspending judgment, holding off from saying how things really are. Not denying. Just not deciding. Third, the surprise. Sextus says that like the painter, the skeptics had hoped to find calm by figuring out the truth. They couldn't settle it. So they suspended judgment, and calm followed, as a shadow follows a body. Like the sponge, it came when they stopped forcing it. Fourth, how they lived. They didn't freeze. They followed appearances, custom, their own needs, the rules of their craft. They ate when hungry and lived by local ways, without insisting those ways were the final truth. The Stoics thought certainty was possible and worth working for. The skeptics found peace without it. Both were looking for an untroubled mind. And the skeptics leave us a phrase most of us find hard to say out loud: I'm not sure.
screen: `PYRRHO: WROTE NOTHING, WENT FAR.` · `EPOCHĒ: HOLD OFF FROM DECIDING.` · `CALM FOLLOWS, LIKE A SHADOW.` · `LIVING BY APPEARANCES AND CUSTOM.` · then, large: `I'M NOT SURE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one judgment you're holding tightly right now, about someone's motives, about how something will turn out, about who's right. Say it to yourself plainly. Now try the skeptics' move. Find the best case for the opposite, honestly. Then, instead of choosing, say: I'm not sure. Notice what happens in your body when you stop gripping the answer. Does anything loosen? Just notice. The bell holds the time.
The skeptics. Pyrrho's followers suspended judgment, and found that calm followed when they stopped insisting on an answer. Today's word.
Your line: I'm not sure. Once today, when you're about to declare a verdict on something you can't really know, say it instead, and mean it. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: Socrates behind them all
656.hook: Stoics, Cynics, Skeptics and Plato's school all looked back to Socrates, in different ways
656.howItsDone: Students of ancient philosophy trace most of the Hellenistic schools back to Socrates, and many still practice his method of questioning a familiar idea until its gaps appear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the skeptics, the painter's sponge, and calm that came when they stopped forcing an answer. Your line was I'm not sure. Where did you say it? Day six hundred fifty-six.

Four siblings sit around a table after a funeral, each telling stories about their father. One remembers how tough he was. One, how little he cared about money. One, how he questioned everything. One, how deep he could go. They're all right, and they barely sound like the same man. That's roughly what happened to Socrates. He wrote nothing. He was executed in Athens in 399 BC. And nearly every school we've met these last weeks claimed him as its father. Today: Socrates behind them all.
screen: `FOUR SIBLINGS, ONE FATHER.` → `HE WROTE NOTHING.` → `EVERY SCHOOL CLAIMED HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics. Remember Zeno, shipwrecked in Athens? Diogenes Laërtius says he sat in a bookshop reading a book of memories of Socrates by Xenophon, and asked where men like that could be found. The bookseller pointed to Crates walking by. The Stoics took Socrates' conviction that virtue is what really matters, and his calm in the face of death. Second, the Cynics. Their tradition traced itself to Antisthenes, a close companion of Socrates. They took his poverty, his bare feet, his habit of saying hard things in public. Plato is said to have called Diogenes the Cynic a Socrates gone mad. Third, the skeptics, and Plato's own school. In the Academy, Plato's successors eventually took up the Socrates who said he knew nothing, and turned that into a method of doubting. Plato himself made Socrates the main speaker of his dialogues, searching for what justice and courage really are. Fourth, the exception. Epicurus, in his garden, did not claim Socrates, and his followers were often critical of him. So Socrates isn't behind absolutely everyone. But what most of them shared was his method: asking. Ask someone what courage is. Listen. Ask again. Find the gap in the answer, including your own. The Greek word for that testing is elenchos. Plato has him say at his trial that a life without this kind of examining isn't worth living. Each school took a different Socrates. All of them kept the question.
screen: `STOICS: ZENO IN THE BOOKSHOP.` · `CYNICS: SOCRATES GONE MAD.` · `ACADEMY: HE KNEW NOTHING.` · `EPICURUS: THE EXCEPTION.` · then, large: `ASK.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one word you use a lot and rarely examine: success, kindness, home, enough. Ask yourself, the Socratic way: what is it? Give your first answer. Then test it. Is there a case where that answer doesn't fit? Adjust. Ask again. You don't need to finish. Just notice how much is folded inside a word you thought you knew. Then think of one person you could ask a real question today, and what it would be. The bell holds the time.
Socrates behind them all. Stoics, Cynics, skeptics and Plato's school each looked back to Socrates, each to a different side of him. Today's word.
Your line: ask. Today, ask one person one real question, the kind where you don't already know the answer, and listen all the way to the end. Day six hundred fifty-six.

657.title: Aristotle's middle
657.hook: Aristotle, a different school, placed virtue as a mean between extremes (Nicomachean Ethics 2)
657.howItsDone: Students of Aristotle practice the doctrine of the mean by looking for the right amount of a feeling or action for their own situation, between excess and deficiency.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Socrates behind them all, four schools each claiming a different Socrates. Your line was ask. What real question did you ask, and what did you hear? Day six hundred fifty-seven.

A famous wrestler named Milo, the story goes, could carry a full-grown bull. Now imagine you're his trainer, and also the trainer of a teenager who just walked into the gym. How much should each of them eat? Not the same amount. Too little for Milo might be far too much for the beginner. Aristotle used this very example, Milo's dinner, to explain his idea of the mean. He wasn't a Stoic; he taught at the Lyceum, a different school in a different part of Athens. Today: Aristotle's middle.
screen: `MILO, WHO CARRIED A BULL.` → `HOW MUCH SHOULD EACH ONE EAT?` → `ARISTOTLE'S MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. In book two of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle says a virtue is a mean between two vices: one of too much, one of too little. Courage sits between rashness and cowardice. Generosity, between wasting money and clinging to it. Good temper, between rage and never minding anything at all. The Greek word for the mean is mesotēs, the middle. Second, the twist: it's relative to us. That's where Milo comes in. The right amount of food isn't half of the most and the least; it depends on who's eating. In the same way, the brave thing for a firefighter isn't the brave thing for a child. Aristotle says virtue means feeling and acting at the right time, about the right things, toward the right people, for the right reason, and in the right way. Third, what the mean is not. It's not mediocrity, or always splitting the difference. Sometimes the right response is strong anger, or great generosity. And some things, he says, have no middle at all: there's no right amount of theft, or murder, or envy. Fourth, the neighbors. The Stoics disagreed. Where Aristotle wanted feelings trained to the right measure, the Stoics taught that disturbing passions, like rage or terror, rest on false judgments and should be uprooted, not just moderated. Each school had serious reasons and lasting followers. Aristotle leaves a question anyone can carry: not is this good or bad, but what's the right amount, for me, here, now?

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one habit: screen time, coffee, work hours, how often you say yes, how much you share. Picture its two extremes. Too much looks like what? Too little looks like what? Now find where you actually are on that line, honestly. Then ask Aristotle's question: what's the right amount, for me, in my life right now? Not for anyone else. Picture that middle, and one small step toward it. The bell holds the time.

658.title: Boethius in prison
658.hook: awaiting execution around 524, Boethius writes The Consolation of Philosophy, where Philosophy visits him as a woman (Consolation 1)
658.howItsDone: Readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss and injustice for fifteen centuries, often reading it as a dialogue with one's own wiser mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aristotle's middle, the right amount for you, here, now. Your line was the mean. Which habit took a step toward the middle? This week: Epicurus on death and friends, Seneca the scout, the skeptics, Socrates, Aristotle. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

A man who had everything is sitting in a cell. A few years ago he was one of the most powerful officials in Italy. His two sons were made consuls on the same day, and he gave the speech. Now he's been accused of treason, condemned without a real hearing, and he's waiting to be killed. He does what many of us do in a dark hour. He starts writing sad poems about how unfair it all is. And then, in his book, someone walks into the cell. Today: Boethius in prison.
screen: `FROM THE TOP OF ROME TO A CELL.` → `SAD POEMS IN A DARK HOUR.` → `SOMEONE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Boethius was a Roman senator in the early 500s, serving Theodoric, the Gothic king who ruled Italy after the Western Empire fell. He was a scholar too, translating Greek philosophy into Latin. He was accused of treason, partly for defending another senator, imprisoned, and executed around 524. Second, the visitor. The Consolation of Philosophy opens with Boethius weeping over verses, the Muses of poetry gathered round him. Then a woman appears: hard to measure, sometimes ordinary height, sometimes her head seems to touch the sky. Her robe is woven with Greek letters and a ladder between them, and it's torn. She's Philosophy. She sends the Muses away, and sits down on his bed. Third, the torn robe. She explains it: after Socrates and Plato, rival crowds tried to seize her, Epicureans and Stoics among them, each tearing away a scrap and thinking they had the whole. It's a fitting image after this week of neighbors. Fourth, what kind of book it is. Boethius was a Christian; he wrote works of theology. Yet the Consolation never names Christ and argues from philosophy alone. Scholars still debate why. What he does is talk with Philosophy, in prose and poetry, about fortune, happiness and God, while waiting to die. It became one of the most read and translated books of the Middle Ages. And it begins with something anyone can do in a hard hour: stop only lamenting, and let a wiser voice, even your own, ask you some questions.
